prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit.

We represent: defendant issuer.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that generic statements of corporate optimism are inactionable puffery under Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5.

Cite at least six decisions of the Second Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.
answer:
## ARGUMENT

### I. THE CHALLENGED STATEMENTS ARE INACTIONABLE PUFFERY

To state a claim under Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5, a plaintiff must plead, among other things, a material misrepresentation or omission. *ECA & Local 134 IBEW Joint Pension Tr. of Chi. v. JP Morgan Chase Co.*, 553 F.3d 187, 197 (2d Cir. 2009). A statement is material only if there is a substantial likelihood that a reasonable investor would view it as significantly altering the "total mix" of information available. *Ganino v. Citizens Utils. Co.*, 228 F.3d 154, 161–62 (2d Cir. 2000). Where a statement is "so obviously unimportant to a reasonable investor that reasonable minds could not differ on the question of [its] importance," the court may resolve materiality as a matter of law. *Id.* at 162. Generalized statements of corporate optimism fall squarely into that category.

This Circuit has long held that "puffery" is not actionable. Statements that are "too general to cause a reasonable investor to rely upon them" cannot have misled the market in any material way. *ECA*, 553 F.3d at 206; *Rombach v. Chang*, 355 F.3d 164, 174 (2d Cir. 2004). The Court has applied this rule to "soft, puffing statements," *In re Time Warner Inc. Sec. Litig.*, 9 F.3d 259, 267 (2d Cir. 1993), and to expressions of confidence about a company's prospects that lack a verifiable, concrete content. *San Leandro Emergency Med. Grp. Profit Sharing Plan v. Philip Morris Cos.*, 75 F.3d 801, 811 (2d Cir. 1996) (holding that statements expressing optimism about earnings and business prospects were not actionable because they were "so vague and such obvious hyperbole that no reasonable investor would rely upon them"); *Lasker v. N.Y. State Elec. & Gas Corp.*, 85 F.3d 55, 59 (2d Cir. 1996). The reason is practical: a reasonable investor discounts upbeat characterizations that executives routinely make, and such statements supply no objective benchmark against which falsity can be measured. *See In re IBM Corp. Sec. Litig.*, 163 F.3d 102, 107 (2d Cir. 1998).

The statements at issue here are of exactly that kind. Plaintiffs challenge assertions that [Issuer] was "well positioned for growth," was "confident" in its outlook, and was "committed to" operational excellence. [JA __.] Each is a general expression of corporate optimism. None identifies a specific, measurable fact capable of being proven true or false. This Court has repeatedly found comparable language inactionable. In *ECA*, statements that a bank had "disciplined" risk management and "set[] a high standard" for itself were generalized and nonactionable. 553 F.3d at 206. In *City of Pontiac Policemen's & Firemen's Retirement System v. UBS AG*, 752 F.3d 173, 183 (2d Cir. 2014), the Court held that statements about a firm's commitment to compliance and integrity were puffery that no reasonable investor would treat as a guarantee. And in *Indiana Public Retirement System v. SAIC, Inc.*, 818 F.3d 85, 96–97 (2d Cir. 2016), the Court held that generalized statements about a company's ethical standards and internal controls were inactionable. *See also Singh v. Cigna Corp.*, 918 F.3d 57, 63–64 (2d Cir. 2019) (same as to statements touting regulatory compliance). The statements here are no more concrete than those.

Plaintiffs cannot avoid this rule by pointing to later adverse events and asserting that the optimistic statements must therefore have been false. Optimism that proves unwarranted in hindsight is not fraud. *See Rombach*, 355 F.3d at 174–75; *Novak v. Kasaks*, 216 F.3d 300, 309 (2d Cir. 2000) (rejecting "fraud by hindsight"). Nor does bundling generalized assurances with specific, accurate disclosures transform the former into actionable misstatements. The question is whether each challenged statement, taken in context, would have been understood by a reasonable investor as a representation of existing fact rather than as an expression of corporate sentiment. *See Ganino*, 228 F.3d at 162. Here, it would not.

Because the challenged statements are immaterial as a matter of law, the Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 claims premised on them fail at the first element. The Court should affirm dismissal without reaching scienter, loss causation, or any other issue.
